prompt: A jar contains only dimes and quarters. There are $30$ coins in all, worth $\$5.70$ total. How many quarters are in the jar?
hint: You know two totals about the jar: how many coins there are and how much they are worth. Each total gives its own equation.

hints.text: You know two totals about the jar: how many coins there are and how much they are worth. Each total gives its own equation.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try fewer coins: $4$ coins of nickels and dimes worth $\$0.35$. All nickels would be $\$0.20$; the $\$0.15$ excess divided by the $\$0.05$ swap value gives $3$ dimes. Same assume-then-adjust logic.
With $d$ dimes and $q$ quarters, $d + q = 30$ and $0.10d + 0.25q = 5.70$. Replace $d$ with $30 - q$ in the value equation and solve for $q$.
The equation becomes $3 + 0.15q = 5.70$, so $0.15q = 2.70$ and $q = 18$. The jar holds $18$ quarters.

learningObjective: Model a count-and-value situation as a system.
explanation: Let $d$ be the number of dimes and $q$ the number of quarters. Counting coins gives $d + q = 30$, and adding values gives $0.10d + 0.25q = 5.70$.
Substitute $d = 30 - q$ into the value equation so only $q$ remains: $0.10(30 - q) + 0.25q = 5.70$.
Distribute and combine like terms: $3 + 0.15q = 5.70$, so $0.15q = 2.70$ and $q = 18$.
Check with $12$ dimes: $12(0.10) + 18(0.25) = 1.20 + 4.50 = 5.70$. The jar contains $18$ quarters.

alternativeExplanations.title: Start from an all-dimes jar
steps: If all $30$ coins were dimes the jar would hold $\$3.00$ — but it holds $\$5.70$, an excess of $\$2.70$.
Swapping one dime for one quarter adds $\$0.15$ to the total.
$\$2.70 \div \$0.15 = 18$ swaps, so there are $18$ quarters. This "assume then adjust" method skips the system entirely.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Answering 12 — the dimes — is the designed miss; both counts appear as choices.
Re-read the final question after solving. The system gives you the pair; the question wants exactly one of them.
